messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sameer, a 41-year-old architect, presented as a man holding himself together with immense effort, his posture rigid and his gaze constantly scanning the room. The trauma occurred eight months prior, but for Sameer, it was a continuous present. The event itself was a brutal culmination of a relationship that had become quietly volatile. His then-partner, Mark, had come home drunk, the smell of whiskey sharp and cloying in their apartment. An argument, fueled by alcohol, had escalated with terrifying speed. Mark’s words slurred into an incomprehensible roar of accusation, and then the violence began. Sameer remembers the attack not as a fluid sequence but as a series of stark, still images, like a slideshow from a nightmare. He sees the glint of the lamp, a fist, the pattern of the rug rushing toward his face. He remembers the feeling of being too sick and dizzy to get up, the world a blur of noise and pain.

In the months that followed, Sameer found that the world had been wired with triggers connected directly to that night. The smell of alcohol is the most potent; at a recent firm reception, a colleague opened a bottle of scotch nearby, and the scent instantly plunged him back into the memory. He saw not his colleague but Mark’s face, contorted with rage, and his body reacted before his mind could catch up. A wave of terror washed over him, his heart hammering against his ribs as if trying to escape, a physical certainty of imminent danger that was utterly disconnected from the safe reality of the reception. This happens constantly; his body is a sentry that has long since abandoned its post in the present, reacting to threats that only it can see.

This state of constant threat has become his new baseline, a high-frequency hum of anxiety that makes ordinary life feel treacherous. He is jumpy, startling violently at the sound of a dropped book or a car backfiring. At his open-plan office, the overlapping conversations of his colleagues often merge into a meaningless, threatening chatter. This auditory chaos doesn't just distract him; it yanks him back to the memory of Mark’s incoherent shouting. The memory, in turn, amplifies his sense of threat, leaving him drenched in the same cold terror he felt on the floor of his old apartment. Because he is always anticipating an attack, his mind is primed to find these echoes everywhere, turning the ambient noise of his workplace into a personal torment. This perpetual state of vigilance makes the intrusive, photographic stills of the assault more frequent and vivid, as if his mind is constantly re-opening the wound to check if it’s still there.

The memories themselves are a source of profound distress. When the snapshots flash into his mind—the raised hand, the shattered glass—they are not just images but full-bodied re-experiences. The terror is immediate and absolute, and it invariably brings with it a cascade of self-recrimination. He sees his own inaction in those frozen moments and is consumed by the belief that he failed. He was betrayed by the person he trusted most, and the memory of that betrayal is inextricably linked to the conviction that he should have seen it coming, should have done something different. This appraisal—that he can’t trust his own judgment—has poisoned his self-concept. The memory of being helpless fuels the present-day belief that he is fundamentally incapable of doing the right thing to protect himself.

This corrosive self-doubt has become the engine of his hypervigilance. The world feels profoundly unsafe to Sameer precisely because he has come to believe he is inadequate to navigate it. The conviction that he failed in his most important role—to keep himself safe—means he cannot trust his own instincts. This forces his body to remain on high alert, a desperate compensation for a mind he no longer trusts. Sleep offers no respite; he lies awake for hours, convinced that he must stay alert for a danger he cannot name but feels in his bones. Even a simple head cold can become a trigger; the feeling of physical unwellness is a direct echo of his helplessness during the assault, and with it comes the crushing thought that he is weak, a failure.

His life has shrunk dramatically. He and his wife, Priya, now sleep in separate rooms because of his inability to rest. He feels he is failing her, a ghost in his own marriage. He finally sought therapy after an incident last week. Priya had tried to comfort him after a loud noise made him cry out, and he flinched away from her touch so violently that she recoiled, her face a mask of hurt. It was in that moment, seeing the pain he was causing the person he loved most, that he realised the trauma was not just living inside him, but was actively destroying the life he had tried so hard to build.
